title: Linear rank tests for location and scale
breadcrumb: Non-parametric methods → Linear rank tests → Location and scale
engineName: Choose scores to match location or scale.
objectives: Define a linear rank statistic using scores assigned to pooled ranks.
Relate Wilcoxon rank-sum scores to the Mann–Whitney U statistic.
Distinguish Ansari–Bradley and Mood scale score patterns.
Select a location or scale test and state its assumptions and direction.

prereq.name: Pooled ranks and rank sums
prereq.why: Linear rank statistics are formed from ranks in the combined sample.

prereq.name: Location and scale
prereq.why: The alternative determines whether scores should respond to ordering or dispersion.

prereq.name: Two-independent-sample design
prereq.why: The standard two-sample linear rank framework assumes independent samples.

traps: A linear rank statistic is T=Σa(Rᵢ); the score function matters.
Wilcoxon rank sum uses a(r)=r; U subtracts n₁(n₁+1)/2.
Ansari–Bradley scores are high near the pooled centre.
Mood scores are high at the pooled extremes.
A scale test is not automatically a test of variance without its centre assumptions.
Interpret a large statistic using the score direction and sample label.
howto: First identify whether the alternative is location or scale. For location, ordinary rank scores increase with rank. For scale, use a score pattern sensitive to centre or tails. State which sample's scores are being added and what a large total means.

sheet: Normal scores (van der Waerden) and Savage scores are alternative location score systems.
Siegel–Tukey ranks from extremes inward for scale comparisons.
Fligner–Killeen ranks absolute deviations from group medians.
Location interpretation of rank-sum is clearest for similarly shaped distributions.
Scale procedures require attention to common centres, symmetry and centring assumptions.
tricks: Ordinary ranks rise with value: location.
Ansari–Bradley rises toward the centre: concentration.
Mood rises toward the tails: dispersion.
shortcuts: Mood = squared distance from rank centre.
remember: Score function must match the alternative.
Always state which sample's score total is being interpreted.

scenes.title: Start with ranks and score functions
scenes.objective: Understand how pooled ranks become a test statistic.

ask.nudge: The position of an observation in the combined ordered sample.

body: A rank test replaces observations with positions in an ordered list. A linear rank statistic assigns a score to each rank and adds the scores for one sample.
The score function is chosen for the scientific alternative. Scores that increase with rank target a location ordering; scores large near the centre or at the extremes can target scale.

items.ask: Why pool observations from two independent samples before ranking?
items.recall: To put both groups on one common ordering.
refresh: A pooled ranking shows where every observation lies relative to observations from both groups. Ranking each sample separately would erase this cross-group ordering.
The combined ranks are the input to a two-sample rank-sum or linear-rank statistic.

items.recall: A shift in the typical position or centre of a distribution.
refresh: A location alternative asks whether one population tends to produce larger or smaller observations than another.
A rank-sum score increasing with rank is sensitive to systematic ordering. A median interpretation is clearest when distribution shapes are comparable.

items.recall: A difference in spread or variability around a centre.
refresh: Two groups can have the same centre but different dispersion. One may be more concentrated and the other more spread out.
A scale test must use information about distance from the centre or extremeness, rather than simply asking which group has larger values.

scenes.title: Location and scale are different alternatives
scenes.objective: See why the score pattern must match the question.

ask.q: If two groups share a centre but one is more dispersed, is this a location or scale question?

body: A location test asks whether observations from one group tend to be higher than observations from another. A scale test asks whether one group is more spread out around its centre.
A single rank score pattern cannot be optimal for every alternative. Linear rank methods make the score choice explicit.

scenario.teaser: Two independent groups and a location alternative.
scenario.title: Comparing typical outcomes
body: A researcher compares an outcome from two independent groups. The question is whether one group tends to have larger values, which is a location question. A linear rank statistic assigns a score to each pooled rank and adds the scores belonging to one group. Choosing ordinary rank scores gives the Wilcoxon rank-sum statistic, which is equivalent to Mann–Whitney U after subtracting a fixed minimum rank sum. Other score systems, such as normal scores, target different location alternatives.
scenario.q: What does the ordinary Wilcoxon rank-sum score do?
scenario.answer: It assigns increasing scores to pooled ranks and sums the ranks belonging to one group.

scenes.title: Look at three score patterns
scenes.objective: Compare location scores with scale scores.

ask.q: Which ranks receive larger Ansari–Bradley scores?
ask.nudge: Ranks near the centre of the pooled ordering.

viz.caption: Location scores rise with rank; scale scores can be largest at the centre or at the extremes.

body: For N=8, ordinary Wilcoxon scores are 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8. Ansari–Bradley scores are 1,2,3,4,4,3,2,1, largest near the centre.
Mood scores are squared distances from the pooled centre (N+1)/2. They are largest at the extremes.

scenes.title: Linear rank statistics for location
scenes.objective: Define the general statistic and the Wilcoxon score choice.

ask.q: What score function gives the Wilcoxon rank-sum statistic?

blocks.body: T=Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ¹ a(Rᵢ), where Rᵢ is a pooled rank and a(r) is the selected score function.
Choose a(r)=r. Then T=R₁, the pooled rank sum for sample 1. Mann–Whitney U₁=R₁−n₁(n₁+1)/2.
Normal scores (van der Waerden) and Savage scores transform rank positions differently and are selected for particular location alternatives.
A large rank-sum statistic indicates sample 1 tends to occupy higher pooled ranks. Direction depends on the sample label and score convention.

flow.title: Choose the score family
flow.alt: A directional shift leads to increasing location scores; a spread difference leads to centre- or tail-sensitive scale scores.
flow.note: The score function must match the alternative.

ask.q: Which score pattern gives high scores near the pooled centre?

blocks.body: For N pooled ranks, a(r)=min(r,N+1−r). Scores are small at both extremes and large near the centre. A more concentrated sample tends to receive a larger score sum.
A(r)=[r−(N+1)/2]². Scores are largest at the extremes and smallest near the centre. A more dispersed sample tends to accumulate larger Mood scores.
Siegel–Tukey assigns ranks from the extremes inward to compare scale. Fligner–Killeen ranks absolute deviations from group medians for a robust scale comparison.
Scale tests generally require comparable centres or a suitable centring step. Check each procedure's symmetry and sampling assumptions before interpreting it as a pure variance test.

scenes.problem: For N=8, Ansari–Bradley scores are 1,2,3,4,4,3,2,1. Sample A occupies ranks 1,2,7,8. Find its score sum.
hints: Read the score for each pooled rank.
Select the four scores for ranks 1,2,7,8.
Add them and compare with the centre ranks.
scenes.answer: The scores are 1, 2, 2 and 1, so the Ansari–Bradley total is 6.
scenes.check: The centre ranks receive larger scores; an extreme-rank sample should have a smaller total.

solution.why: The score function is symmetric around the pooled centre.
This is the score sum for sample A.
Ansari–Bradley scores are largest near the centre.

scenario.teaser: Two production lines have similar centres but possibly different spread.
scenario.title: Comparing process variability
body: A quality team compares variability in two independent production lines. The group centres are similar, but one line may have more spread. A scale test should respond to how far observations lie from the centre, not simply whether one group has larger values. Ansari–Bradley gives larger scores to central pooled ranks, while Mood's scale test gives larger scores to ranks far from the pooled centre. The score pattern must match the alternative being tested.
scenario.q: Which score family gives high scores to central pooled ranks?

scenes.title: Six statements to challenge
scenes.intro: Mark each claim true or false before revealing the reason.

items.claim: A linear rank statistic sums scores assigned to pooled ranks.
items.why: True. T=Σa(Rᵢ) for the observations in the selected sample.
True. The score is the pooled rank itself.

items.claim: Mann–Whitney U equals the Wilcoxon rank sum R₁.
Ansari–Bradley scores are largest near the pooled centre.
items.why: True. The score min(r,N+1−r) is centre-sensitive.

items.claim: Mood scale scores are largest at the extremes.
items.why: True. Mood uses squared distance from the pooled rank centre.

items.claim: A scale test can always be interpreted as a pure variance test without checking centre assumptions.
items.why: False. Scale-test interpretation depends on centring and shape assumptions.

scenes.title: Guided calculation: a quick numeric check
scenes.objective: Calculate a statistic only after identifying its test.
scenes.problem: Study A asks whether one independent group tends to have larger values than another. Study B asks whether two groups with similar centres differ in spread. Which score family is appropriate for each?
hints: Study A is a location alternative.
Study B is a scale alternative.
Choose increasing rank scores for location and centre/tail-sensitive scores for scale.
scenes.answer: Study A: Wilcoxon rank-sum/Mann–Whitney or another location score system. Study B: Ansari–Bradley or Mood, with assumptions checked.
scenes.check: Do not choose a location rank-sum solely because it is familiar when the target is spread.

solution.why: The alternative is directional ordering in pooled ranks.
The test must respond to distance from the centre or extremeness.
Their scores target dispersion rather than a simple location shift.

scenes.title: Assumptions and interpretation
scenes.objective: State what a rank-score result can support.

ask.q: Why check score direction before interpreting a large statistic?
ask.nudge: The score function and sample label determine which alternative produces a large value.

blocks.body: Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney compares independent distributions through pooled ordering. A simple median-shift interpretation is strongest when distributions have similar shapes.
Ansari–Bradley and Mood target spread differences under their stated conditions. Check whether groups share a centre or whether the procedure uses a suitable centring step.
Name the target (location or scale), state the design (independent or paired), identify the score pattern, and explain what a large statistic means for the labelled sample.

items.a: Whether the alternative concerns location or scale.
